subject: Accounting
title: The Journalist's Role
description: A quick win: understand The Journalist's Role.

hook.text: A Financial Times reporter spent years investigating Wirecard. The company sued. He kept digging.

buildup.text: Dan McCrum published article after article showing holes in Wirecard's financial statements.

discovery.text: Investigative journalists often spot fraud before regulators because they ask uncomfortable questions.

twist.text: German regulators banned short selling of Wirecard stock and investigated McCrum instead.

climax.text: When Wirecard collapsed, McCrum's reporting was vindicated. He won multiple journalism awards.

punchline.text: The pen exposed what auditors missed.

quiz.question: How did German regulators initially respond to Wirecard reporting?
options: They investigated the journalist instead of Wirecard

details.summary: Investigative journalists have been instrumental in exposing some of the biggest accounting frauds—often publishing evidence before regulators acted. This topic covers landmark reporting that brought down fraudulent companies and the vital role of a free press in financial markets.
details.whyItMatters: When auditors miss fraud and regulators are slow, journalists become the last line of defense for investors. Financial investigative reporting protects markets by holding powerful companies accountable.
takeaways: Bethany McLean's Fortune article 'Is Enron Overpriced?' was one of the first to question Enron publicly
The Financial Times' investigation of Wirecard lasted years before regulators took action
Journalists often face legal threats and intimidation from companies they investigate

faq.question: How have journalists helped expose accounting fraud?
faq.answer: Journalists have broken stories that led to major fraud investigations. Bethany McLean questioned Enron's business model in Fortune. The Financial Times pursued Wirecard for years. Reporters often identify red flags months or years before regulators act.

faq.question: Why do journalists sometimes catch fraud before regulators?
faq.answer: Journalists can investigate based on tips, hunches, and publicly available information without needing the legal authority or formal complaints that regulators require. They can publish findings quickly, while regulatory investigations take months or years to complete.
